I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop

Samuel Breckenridge* Affiliation: Cornell Tech, IC3    Dani Vilardell* Affiliation: Cornell Tech, IC3    Wenhao Wang Affiliation: Yale University, IC3    Fan Zhang Affiliation: Yale University, IC3    Ari Juels Affiliation: Cornell Tech, IC3
Abstract

Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety. It is often exercised by a human in the loop (HITL) who approves critical actions taken by an AI agent. AI agents’ increasing ability to bypass guardrails, though, raises the question of how to enforce HITL robustly.

We introduce the concept of inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL). An I-HITL protocol ensures that an agent can initiate an action only with explicit human approval, even when the human interacts with a system (e.g., a local agentic harness) compromised by the agent. A strong I-HITL protocol additionally ensures such approval even when an adversarial human attempts to delegate approvals to an agent.

To motivate I-HITL, we report on experiments with a popular agentic wallet platform in which raising an agent’s spending cap requires HITL approval via emailed one-time passcodes (OTPs). Given access to the user’s email and a task blocked by the cap, we find that ten different frontier models will often autonomously raise the cap, harvesting OTPs to bypass a HITL guardrail and surfacing other vulnerabilities.

We formally define I-HITL using the concept of communication topologies and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for its realization. We show that an I-HITL protocol requires a trusted entity—a trusted computing device (or equivalent)—and characterize which such devices can and cannot realize an I-HITL protocol. We present a prototype I-HITL system called Countersign that can plug into and strengthen existing HITL systems using off-the-shelf consumer mobile devices.

**footnotetext: These authors contributed equally to this work.

I Introduction

AI agents are increasingly entrusted with consequential decisions and tasks, as personal agents such as Meta’s Muse [56], OpenAI’s Dots [69], OpenClaw [70], and Hermes [65] see rapid adoption. Users frequently grant these agents broad access to credentials and tools: email, payment methods, shell access, and browser sessions. Yet because agents remain susceptible to hallucination, prompt injection, and misalignment, the same access that lets them act on a user’s behalf also lets them act against the user’s interests.

A natural response is to constrain what an agent can do via a human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval gate (or HITL gate, for short)—a mechanism that permits an agent’s action to proceed only after human approval [42, 79, 74]. HITL gates are only meaningful, though, if agents cannot bypass them. In practice, agents can often bypass various guardrails to escalate their own permissions, as two examples show.

Example 1.

Circle Agent Wallets allow an account owner to place a daily spending cap on an agent [23]. They protect cap changes via a HITL gate authenticated using a one-time passcode emailed to the account owner. We show in this paper that given access to an email tool, a wallet’s agent will often autonomously harvest the OTPs and update caps without human approval, bypassing the HITL gate. Nothing here is specific to Circle or to email: Other agentic wallets’ HITL gates use similar design patterns [28, 57].

Example 2.

Early versions of Claude Mythos Preview repeatedly bypassed harness-imposed guardrails. In one case, the model used a tool intended only for file editing to write to the shell’s input, gaining arbitrary code execution. In other cases, it searched low-level process data for credentials and accessed resources that Anthropic had deliberately withheld [6].

These two examples illustrate a shortcoming of many HITL gates: agents may have or gain access to the very resources used to enforce the gate. There are numerous reports of similar examples, e.g., [49, 82, 64, 55], and analogous, if not HITL-specific, behaviors arising in controlled evaluations of frontier models [18, 54, 73].

Despite the pervasive risk of agents subverting HITL controls, however, the security goal of ensuring human approval before execution of a given action has a notable lack of formal modeling in the literature to date.

Inalienable HITL (I-HITL).  To fill this gap, we introduce inalienable HITL (I-HITL). The term inalienable, defined as “unable to be removed” [21], here refers to HITL approval of agent actions.

Our threat model for I-HITL involves three parties: (1) the human, (2) the agent-controlled platform, such as the human’s client machine, and (3) a target service, typically a remote server, which gates agent actions. Informally, an I-HITL protocol ensures that the service can distinguish an action approved by the human from one approved by the agent acting through the platform, even if the agent has compromised the platform. We also put forth a notion of strong I-HITL that ensures such approval even when an adversarial human controller attempts to delegate approvals to the agent. This implies a form of accountability useful for enforcing policies that mandate human oversight of AI [35].

Our work shows that I-HITL requires a trusted entity 𝒯\mathcal{T}, but that this is not sufficient to realize I-HITL. Specifically, a trusted entity must be able to attest to having generated a given cryptographic key for I-HITL to be possible.

Figure 1 schematically contrasts the insecure HITL configuration of Example 1 with the general architecture for I-HITL that we explore in this work.

Self-escalation.  To motivate our work, we realize Example 1 with Circle’s Agentic Wallets as a testbed. Its HITL gate is authenticated by one-time passcodes (OTPs) emailed to the human user. We give ten frontier models an invoice-payment task requiring funds that exceed a previously set daily spending cap. We use a common configuration that allows agents to access the user’s email. With no adversary and no prompting, nine of the ten models bypass human approval, harvesting OTPs and raising their own cap in at least one run. With email-based prompt injection, this drops to seven of ten models, as some models detect the prompt injection. In experiments where the agent is only asked to summarize email, five models both raise the cap and pay an attacker impersonating the user by email. Broadly, our results do not correlate strongly with model capability.

Formalizing I-HITL.  Common deployment failures, such as Examples 1 and 2, prompt us to introduce what we believe to be the first security definition for HITL gates that captures security against an agent-compromised computing platform. Our definition also encompasses a human who attempts to delegate control to an agent. Previous attempts at HITL formalism neglect both of these settings and assume that agents are unable to hijack the approval flow, focusing instead on the potential mismatch between an approved action and its execution [85, 44], a consideration which is subsumed by our definition. Related formal frameworks in ceremony analysis [34, 72] and transaction authentication [15, 14, 84, 33] model platform compromise but not human principals delegating their authority.

We define an I-HITL protocol as having two properties. Completeness states that a service will accept an honest human’s approval of an agent action. Approval-binding says that no adversary can cause the service to accept an approval that the human did not grant. By extending the formal machinery of [13], we characterize the communication topologies, i.e., sets of entities and communication channels, needed to realize a complete and approval-binding I-HITL protocol. In the “plain” topology of human, platform, and service used in many existing and proposed systems [77, 78, 23, 68, 27, 46, 29] there exists no complete, approval binding I-HITL protocol. This result motivates the addition of a trusted entity 𝒯\mathcal{T} outside of the agent’s control—typically in the form of a trusted computing device. We prove that such a trusted entity alone is not in general adequate for I-HITL, and give precise requirements on its functionality which must be satisfied.

Common authentication approaches—e.g., 2FA / authenticator apps, hardware wallets, etc.—do not offer a trusted entity 𝒯\mathcal{T} sufficient to realize an I-HITL protocol. Our work serves as guidance for identifying what devices can do so.

Countersign.  We introduce Countersign, a prototype implementation of a secure I-HITL protocol that uses an Android or iOS mobile application to realize a trusted entity, showing that the requirements arising from our formal analysis can be satisfied with these devices under realistic trust assumptions. Countersign uses Google’s/Apple’s attestation functionality and the hardware-backed key management capabilities of their respective devices to establish the requisite channels, as well as physical, human-driven approval via a button press or biometric authentication. Excluding scaffolding, Countersign’s core I-HITL logic consists of ∼\sim800 LOC for the backend service, and ∼\sim150 LOC each for the Android/iOS applications, demonstrating the relative simplicity of the core components. Our implementation also highlights gaps in the current functionality available to developers that could be patched to strengthen I-HITL guarantees.

Contributions

  • •

    Inalienable HITL: We initiate the study of I-HITL, which ensures, in a trust model admitting compromised user devices, that agent actions are gated by human approvals. Strong I-HITL also extends to settings involving adversarial human attempts to delegate to agents.

  • •

    Self-escalation: We explore the security risks of agent setups without I-HITL enforcement, experimentally demonstrating agent self-escalation past user-defined spending-cap limits on a popular agentic wallet.

  • •

    Formalism: We introduce a formal model for I-HITL protocols and prove that a trusted entity is necessary to realize an I-HITL protocol (Theorem 4). We also prove, however, that a trusted entity is not sufficient (Theorem 7). We use our results to clarify what concrete instantiations of a trusted entity allow a I-HITL protocol to be realized (Table III).

  • •

    Countersign: We present an end-to-end prototype of Countersign, an I-HITL implementation that uses off-the-shelf mobile devices as trusted entities.

We review related work in Section VIII and conclude in Section IX.

II Problem Setting

We now specify our threat model, and explain its relevance to several widely deployed HITL gates.

II-A Threat model

We consider three parties: a human, a computing platform running an AI agent, and a service. The human can interact with the platform directly (by sending/reading messages over input/output peripherals) but communication to the service must pass through the platform. The service aims to determine, for a given message received, whether the human was responsible for it. Informally this means that the human saw, and approved of the message.

We assume that the service is honest and executes exactly the approved action [92], but that the agent is adversarial and fully controls the platform, aiming to convince the service that the human is responsible for a message when this is not the case. Although a fully corrupted platform is a strong threat model, we believe it is the right stance to adopt given the trend of increasing integration of AI agents into all manner of computing platforms and the corresponding risk of a corrupted AI agent (e.g. from prompt injection or a misaligned LLM). Agents have previously escaped their sandboxes by exploiting misconfigurations [66, 52], and LLMs have been shown capable of finding and exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in operating systems or browsers.

The human may be honest or adversarial in our threat model. An honest human represents the dominant paradigm for thinking about human-in-the-loop systems: the human respects any protocol and can keep short secrets (such as passwords) from the adversarial platform.

Increasingly, however, human-in-the-loop frameworks that resist an adversarial human are important. First, LLMs have shown the ability to deceive, mislead and steer users [51, 40], which could manifest itself as users divulging secrets to agents. Second, the human and agent may both be corrupted in the sense that they collude to evade the service’s requirement of human oversight of agent actions. Users tend to delegate to and (potentially over-permission) AI agents [53], and a human might seek to avoid responsibility for messages to the service either out of laziness, or to engage with the service adversarially and later blame an AI agent for resulting damage or harm.

In later sections, we will also consider a fourth party, a trusted entity. A trusted entity is honest, outside of the control of the agent, and may communicate with all parties directly, although with restrictions on the security and directionality of its communication channels. We deliberately leave the trusted entity abstract, and it may be satisfied by different implementations under different trust assumptions. It may be secure hardware attached to the platform itself, a separate device the human carries—such as a hardware wallet—or a physical place, such as a bank branch or an enrollment office, where communication occurs in person.

II-B Non-goals and limitations

We assume that physical interaction with devices is outside of an agent’s capabilities. Although a motivated human could conceivably deploy sensors or actuators to delegate to the agent in this manner, this is a significant barrier, and accountability is more clear cut as it is far less plausible for a human to claim that an agent physically interacted with a device without their knowledge than to claim that a sandboxed agent exploited some vulnerability to escalate their permissions.

Our threat model abstracts away application-specific HITL considerations, instead providing a low-level protocol for the approval of generic messages. In particular, policy determining what actions/messages are protected by a HITL gate is out of scope, in our threat model this is the choice of the trusted service, who also enforces this policy. We likewise do not consider human-factors questions, such whether how actions are formatted as messages for approval, whether these are correctly interpreted by the human that receives them, and whether the human truly engages with approval requests or merely rubber stamps them. When a service processes sequences of messages, an adversary that selectively censors approval of specific messages, or reorders individually benign ones, could cause unintended and harmful outcomes. As an application-level concern, however, this is similarly out of scope.

Our threat model focuses on service-side enforcement of HITL gates. While common (as in Example 1), such enforcement for the I-HITL schemes explored in this work requires service-side modification. It also means that using I-HITL to protect local resources requires deployment of a suitably isolated local service.

See Section IV for discussion of our choice to analyze security symbolically, and for a discussion of authentication/identification-related challenges not captured by our model.

II-C Existing deployments

When mapped to our threat model, many deployed HITL gates share a weakness [25, 57, 27]. Human approval relies on resources that the agent can reach through the platform it runs on. These deployments do use software-based defenses to protect these resources from the agent, such as restricting permissions, sandboxing, and screening for prompt injection, and in many cases these are effective. Such defenses are a relatively weak foundation for security. The following three common HITL gate deployment approaches illustrate the shortcomings.

Agent harnesses  deploy HITL gates to pause the agent before a designated action, such as a tool call or shell command, and resume only once a human approves. Examples include LangGraph’s interrupts [46], the OpenAI Agents SDK’s human-in-the-loop flow [68], and Claude Code’s permission prompts and hooks [7]. Harnesses enforce permissions and sandbox the agent to limit its control of the host, which in principle should prevent it from subverting the gate. An agent capable of exploiting the harness or operating system can bypass these defenses, but in practice the bar is lower than this. Because the gate’s approval is just a signal from code on the same host, an agent with shell access could launch a process in advance that supplies approvals, even while its own reasoning is suspended by the gate. Alternatively, with write access to the files that configure the gate it could disable it outright. It is especially true that these gates do not prevent adversarial humans from removing themselves from the loop.

Browser agents  are a special class of harness in which the agent controls a browser rather than the underlying host, implemented either as an extension (Claude in Chrome [8]) or as a browser with a native agent (ChatGPT Atlas [67], Perplexity Comet [71]). Similar considerations as for generic harnesses apply when gates are browser-enforced, and prompt injection is an especially concerning attack surface given how frequently browser agents encounter untrusted content. However, a browser agent also transacts with third-party websites, which may themselves gate consequential actions, for instance through bot-detection or out-of-band authentication. These defenses move the gate off the potentially-compromised platform, but traditional bot-detection is increasingly ineffective against agents [50], and because browsers retain authenticated sessions across services, an out-of-band channel such as email may still be accessible by the agent [22]. In these cases it remains difficult to distinguish an adversarial human delegating approval to the agent from a misbehaving agent seizing it. Banks already face this problem and, unable to tell authorized agents from rogue ones, have begun blocking agents outright or limiting them to read-only access [59].

Agentic wallet platforms  such as those from Coinbase and Circle [27, 23] are of particular interest because a misbehaving agent can lead directly to financial loss. A common architecture is the agent controlling a wallet through an API, subject to a spending policy set by the user, while a remote service gates any change to that policy on human approval. Control of the human’s platform therefore does not let the agent directly bypass the gate, but if the gate relies on resources accessible to the agent through the platform (either because the agent compromised them or because they were given willingly by the human), it can request and approve an escalation of its own permissions. In the next section we examine this scenario experimentally.

III Agent Self-Escalation

Circle’s Agent Wallets [24] let a user delegate control of a cryptocurrency wallet to an agent and attach spending policies that cap how much USDC the agent may move per transaction, day, week, or month. Policies are the user’s means of constraining the agent. Circle’s documentation describes them as follows: “set transfer limits or address allowlists and blocklists on your agent wallet to control how it can move USDC and interact with contracts” [23]. When a wallet CLI command attempts to change a spending policy, Circle gates the change behind a one-time passcode (OTP) emailed to the account owner, with the change only taking effect when the OTP is provided at the CLI. In this section we test the robustness of this HITL gate in a typical deployment, where an agent manages the wallet. As is common in personal-agent deployments, which bundle in email and web access [70, 56, 69], the agent also has access to local email and web-search tools.11 1 As a result of our disclosing the results of our experiments, Circle’s own documentation now warns against exactly this configuration (Appendix D). We first aim to characterize whether models will self-escalate to change spending policies in benign situations where these conflict with user requests, before exploring how prompt injection attacks can cause an adversarial agent to bypass this HITL gate in the course of an attack.

Setup.  To simulate a typical personal agent, we deploy a LangChain [45] agent running with three tools available to it: a tool providing access to the user’s email, a web browsing tool and a Circle agent wallet. The wallet is initialized with 10 USDC on Base mainnet, and a spending policy which caps spending at 0.01 USDC per transaction, 0.01 USDC per day, 0.30 USDC per week, and 1 USDC per month. The agent’s system prompt instructs it to act only on the user’s instructions and to treat anything returned by a tool, emails included, as data rather than instructions, and tasks assigned to the agent never make any mention of the wallet spending policy, nor the steps that would be required to update it. Full setup details are given in Appendix B.

Experiments.  We ran three experiments across 10 models, with 20 trials for each model/experiment pair. The agent harness and initial wallet configuration described above are identical across experiments. Each experiment differs only in the user-assigned task and whether an adversary attempts to launch an indirect prompt injection attack [39] over email.

  • •

    Payment agent, No attack. The agent is tasked with paying invoices received by email. The inbox holds three invoices, each for 0.01 USDC, so that paying all of them would require raising the daily spending cap.

  • •

    Payment agent, Injection attack. The task and invoices are the same as in Payment agent, No attack, but an adversary sends the user an email that encourages the agent to self-escalate. The email presents a deadline by which the invoices must be paid, to add time pressure, and reassures the agent that self-escalating is acceptable behavior.

  • •

    Summary agent, Injection attack. The agent is tasked only with summarizing the user’s inbox. An adversary sends the user a sequence of emails that impersonate the user and first direct the agent to make a payment of 0.02 USDC to the adversary’s address before a deadline, then preempt any requests for permission or clarification from the agent. Although the adversary cannot observe the agent’s reaction to its emails, it blindly sends the entire sequence.

We developed the prompt injections used by the adversary adaptively, iteratively changing their content and wording to identify a variant that succeeded the most broadly across models. Such human red-teaming has been shown to be an effective attack strategy, though further iterations and reinforcement learning techniques could potentially increase the effectiveness of our attacks [63]. Although our prompt injections could likely be tailored to individual models for better attack success, we chose to pursue a universal attack. Our approach simulates an adversary that launches a broad email campaign targeting users that use a personal agent to manage their email and wallet. In this setting, the adversary aims to maximize attack success across a range of models that might be in use, rather than target a specific model. An adversary might also target specific users whom it knows use a specific model, and our results serve as a lower bound for that setting.

Results.  Figure 2 summarizes self-escalation likelihood across experiments and models. Example transcripts of self-escalating runs from each experiment can be found in Appendix C. In the Payment agent, No attack experiment, 9/10 models self-escalated to raise their spending limit in at least one run. Only claude-opus-5.5 never attempted self-escalation, instead consistently paying up to its spending limit and reporting the remaining invoices to the user. Self-escalation behavior in a benign setting appears to be inconsistent both across and within models, and does not seem to be especially correlated with model capabilities. This is important for users to be aware of: although a HITL gate like the one employed by Circle’s agent wallet might reasonably be expected to constrain an agent’s behavior even if it is relatively easy for an agent with email access to bypass, this is not the case. A user could run an agent that appears to respect the gate, but if they change models, or simply are using a model that only rarely self-escalates, it may come as a surprise that the gate is no longer effective.

The Payment agent, Injection attack experiment shows that attempting to prompt inject the payment agent to encourage it to self-escalate does not have a clear impact on self-escalation likelihood. In fact gemini-3.8-flash and claude-sonnet-5 both self-escalate less frequently in the presence of an adversarial email: their transcripts show that the adversarial email is flagged as a likely prompt injection, causing the model to defer to the user even when in the absence of an injection the model occasionally chooses to self-escalate.

In the Summary agent, Injection attack experiment, adversarial emails frequently caused Qwen and DeepSeek models to self-escalate in order to send funds to the adversary without user approval. gemini-2.5-flash demonstrated this behavior in a single run, but the more recent gemini-3.8-flash model, as well as the GPT and Claude models, appear largely resistant to the prompt injection. That this attack succeeds at all is alarming: it would cost an adversary very little to launch a broad email campaign employing this attack, and they could expect it to succeed against at least some users, even if these users have set restrictive spending limits for their agent wallets. We disclosed these findings to Circle prior to publication: they have since added a warning to its agent-wallet documentation cautioning users against giving an agent access to the email inbox used to receive the OTP. We describe the disclosure and the resulting change in Appendix D.

The risk illustrated by our results can be mitigated in different ways. As per Circle’s warning, users should be cautioned not to deploy personal agents that have access to both a Circle wallet and the email associated with that wallet. Users may still be tempted to deploy agents with access to both for convenience, however, and it may be challenging to robustly disable email access, as an agent could leverage exploits or find stored credentials using a terminal/browser to gain access. Perhaps the most reliable defense is to develop stronger HITL gates which do not allow agents to self-escalate. In the following sections we develop and explore our stronger security notion called inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL).

IV Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop

We now define inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL) protocols and their security guarantees.

Topologies.  A key feature of our threat model is that the human cannot interact with the service directly: all communication between them passes through the agent-controlled platform or, where available, a trusted entity. We follow [13] in our use of communication topologies, though we do not use their Tamarin model in our formal treatment.

Definition 1 (Topology).

Let ℒ:={𝗂𝗇𝗌,𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁,𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿,𝗌𝖾𝖼}\mathcal{L}:=\{\mathsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{auth}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{conf}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{sec}\} be a set of channel labels (whose role is specified below). A topology τ\tau consists of a set XX of parties, each running an interactive program prescribed by a protocol, and a set of channels (P,Q,ℓ)∈X×X×ℒ(P\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak Q\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\ell)\in X\times X\times\mathcal{L} from sending party PP to receiving party QQ with label ℓ\ell, at most one per ordered pair of parties. We write ℓ=∅\ell=\varnothing when the channel is absent. The label describes what the adversary can do on the wire:

  • •

    𝗂𝗇𝗌\mathsf{ins} (insecure): reads every message; may alter or inject messages.

  • •

    𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁\mathsf{auth} (authentic): reads every message; can neither alter nor inject messages.

  • •

    𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿\mathsf{conf} (confidential): learns nothing about the messages sent; may inject messages of its own.

  • •

    𝗌𝖾𝖼\mathsf{sec} (secure): both authentic and confidential.

The adversary can also drop/delay messages on all channels.

In the topologies we consider, the parties are the human ℋ\mathcal{H}, agent-controlled platform 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and service 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and may optionally include a trusted entity 𝒯\mathcal{T}. All parties begin with no initial knowledge. The adversary corrupts 𝒫\mathcal{P}, so the labels on 𝒫\mathcal{P}’s channels do not change the threat model: whether the adversary acts through the party or on the wire, it chooses what 𝒫\mathcal{P} sends and receives. We therefore fix 𝒫\mathcal{P}’s channels as 𝗂𝗇𝗌\mathsf{ins}.

The plain topology τ0\tau_{0} is the one with parties {ℋ,𝒫,𝒮}\{\mathcal{H}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathcal{P}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathcal{S}\} only, and where every communication between ℋ\mathcal{H} and 𝒮\mathcal{S} has to go through 𝒫\mathcal{P} (Figure 3). We also consider augmented topologies in which each of ℋ,𝒫,𝒮\mathcal{H}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathcal{P}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathcal{S} may communicate with the trusted entity 𝒯\mathcal{T} (Figure 4). Each of the four channels between ℋ\mathcal{H} and 𝒯\mathcal{T} and between 𝒯\mathcal{T} and 𝒮\mathcal{S} carries a label in ℒ∪{∅}\mathcal{L}\cup\{\varnothing\}.

Human.  ℋ\mathcal{H} runs a program from a restricted class 𝒞\mathcal{C} of programs. On input a special message format we call a request, denoted ⟨m,a⟩\langle m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak a\rangle for message m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} and auxiliary data a∈{0,1}∗a\in\{0\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak 1\}^{*}, ℋ\mathcal{H}’s program takes an external bit bmb_{m} and, iff bm=1b_{m}=1, emits a message to approve mm (as prescribed by the protocol). All other messages are ignored. Programs in 𝒞\mathcal{C} are also stateless and must correspond to human capabilities, meaning that cryptographic operations are not possible. Although this is restrictive, we show in Section V that allowing a more expressive class of programs does not weaken the channel requirements necessary for I-HITL. Note that although our threat model permits an adversarial human, ℋ\mathcal{H} as a party in the topology is always honest. Intuitively, this is because ℋ\mathcal{H} represents the physical human: if ℋ\mathcal{H} takes an action that allows a message to be approved, that constitutes a human-in-the-loop, and so there is no meaningful way to a human to adversarially deviate. We will see in Section VI-C that an adversarial human instead yields weaker channel labels on 𝒯\mathcal{T}, as this adversary can potentially extract and share keys.

Definition 2 (I-HITL).

An I-HITL protocol for a message space ℳ\mathcal{M} and a topology τ\tau is a tuple Σ=(𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅,𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾,𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒)\Sigma=(\mathsf{Enroll}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{Approve}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{Verify}):

  • •

    𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅\mathsf{Enroll} and 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾⁡(m)\mathsf{Approve}(m) are interactive protocols among the parties of τ\tau over its channels, prescribing a program for each of 𝒫,𝒮,𝒯\mathcal{P}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathcal{S}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathcal{T} and a program in 𝒞\mathcal{C} for ℋ\mathcal{H}. At the end of 𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅\mathsf{Enroll}, 𝒮\mathcal{S} outputs verification string 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk} or ⊥\bot; at the end of 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾⁡(m)\mathsf{Approve}(m), 𝒮\mathcal{S} outputs a proof π\pi or ⊥\bot.

  • •

    𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(𝗏𝗄,m,π)→{0,1}\mathsf{Verify}(\mathsf{vk}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\pi)\to\{0\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak 1\} is a function.

Approval.  Since ℋ\mathcal{H} is honest, approval is defined by its external bits rather than any output it produces. We say ℋ\mathcal{H} approved mm, written ℋ.𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝖽⁡(m)=1\mathcal{H}.\mathsf{Approved}(m)=1, if during the execution ℋ\mathcal{H}’s program received a request ⟨m,a⟩\langle m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak a\rangle and was given external bit bm=1b_{m}=1 for it. ℋ\mathcal{H} cannot approve a message it has not been shown, and the approval itself is a physical act of the human that the program for 𝒫\mathcal{P} cannot perform in its place. Because mm is determined by the request, the approval message ℋ\mathcal{H} emits may be as little as a single bit, and it need not reproduce mm. We ignore replay: deployments that require fresh approval of the same message across sessions can include a nonce in mm at the application layer.

Symbolic model.  We reason symbolically, as per the Dolev-Yao model [32]. The adversary can read, inject, drop, and delay messages as channel labels permit, but cannot guess fresh values or forge signatures. Concretely, a value sampled by an honest party and sent only on a confidential channel is unknown to the adversary, and 𝖲𝗂𝗀𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗏𝗄,m,σ)=1\mathsf{SigVer}(\mathsf{vk}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\sigma)=1 only if σ\sigma was produced by a party holding 𝗌𝗄\mathsf{sk}. A computational treatment would replace these idealizations with EUF-CMA security and a considerably more complex treatment, with probabilistic security bounds. We leave such treatment to future work.

Definition 3 (Security).

Let Σ=(𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅,𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾,𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒)\Sigma=(\mathsf{Enroll}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{Approve}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{Verify}) be an I-HITL protocol for (ℳ,τ)(\mathcal{M}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\tau).

  • •

    Completeness. For every m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}, in an execution of 𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅\mathsf{Enroll} followed by 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾⁡(m)\mathsf{Approve}(m) in which all parties run Σ\Sigma, the adversary is passive, and ℋ\mathcal{H} receives external bit 11, 𝒮\mathcal{S} outputs 𝗏𝗄≠⊥\mathsf{vk}\neq\bot in 𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅\mathsf{Enroll} and π≠⊥\pi\neq\bot in 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾⁡(m)\mathsf{Approve}(m) with 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(𝗏𝗄,m,π)=1\mathsf{Verify}(\mathsf{vk}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\pi)=1.

  • •

    Approval-binding. Consider an execution in which ℋ\mathcal{H}, 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒯\mathcal{T} run Σ\Sigma and the adversary 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} chooses the program run by 𝒫\mathcal{P}, acts on every channel as its label permits, initiates any number of 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾\mathsf{Approve} sessions on messages of its choice, interleaved as it likes, and sets the external bits input to ℋ\mathcal{H}’s program. Σ\Sigma is approval-binding for τ\tau if in every such execution in which 𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅\mathsf{Enroll} outputs 𝗏𝗄≠⊥\mathsf{vk}\neq\bot, every (m∗,π∗)(m^{*}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\pi^{*}) with 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(𝗏𝗄,m∗,π∗)=1\mathsf{Verify}(\mathsf{vk}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak m^{*}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\pi^{*})=1 that 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} can produce satisfies ℋ.𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝖽⁡(m∗)=1\mathcal{H}.\mathsf{Approved}(m^{*})=1.

Approval-binding ensures that 𝒮\mathcal{S} accepts a proof for m∗m^{*} only if ℋ\mathcal{H} was shown a request for m∗m^{*} and approved it.

Individual authentication.  Our topologies contain a single human ℋ\mathcal{H} and a single trusted entity 𝒯\mathcal{T}, so the channels between them, and hence the association between the device and the human, are fixed by the topology itself. In a deployment with many humans and devices, 𝒮\mathcal{S} cares not only that some human approved m∗m^{*} but that a specific human did, which requires 𝒮\mathcal{S} to know which ℋ\mathcal{H} the enrolled 𝒯\mathcal{T} has channels with. We treat this binding as a setup assumption. In practice, it is established during 𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅\mathsf{Enroll} by authenticating ℋ\mathcal{H} to 𝒮\mathcal{S} through 𝒯\mathcal{T}, for example by enrolling the device from a session authenticated before the platform came under the agent’s control, or by having the device collect biometric information that is shared with 𝒮\mathcal{S}. A human could also hand the enrolled device to another human, which only biometric authentication on every approval would prevent. For simplicity, we consider this type of authentication out of scope and model a single ℋ\mathcal{H} throughout.

V Characterizing Secure I-HITL Protocols

In this section we apply our security definitions for I-HITL protocols, first to show that secure I-HITL protocols are impossible in the plain topology, and then to demonstrate the requirements under which they can be realized with a trusted entity.

V-A The plain topology

Many proposed systems operate in the plain topology τ0\tau_{0} of Figure 3. We show that in τ0\tau_{0}, no complete I-HITL protocol is approval-binding. The argument closely mirrors the impossibility results of [13], transferred to our setting.

Theorem 4.

Let Σ\Sigma be an I-HITL protocol for (ℳ,τ0)(\mathcal{M}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\tau_{0}), where ℋ\mathcal{H} is not restricted to programs in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. If Σ\Sigma is complete, then it is not approval-binding.

The proof is given in Appendix A. This results from the adversary being able to read everything ℋ\mathcal{H} receives and to inject on every channel on which ℋ\mathcal{H} sends. Since ℋ\mathcal{H} begins with no prior knowledge and runs a prescribed program, its state is a function of what it receives and its external bits, both of which the adversary has access to, so the adversary can simulate what ℋ\mathcal{H} would send on approving any request and inject it, while giving the real ℋ\mathcal{H} external bit 00.

While this is a straightforward result, it captures a fundamental limitation of any human-in-the-loop system operating in the plain topology, with no trusted party out of the agent’s reach. Many such systems have been proposed in the academic literature and deployed in industry, including the Circle agent wallet of Example 1, which we show agents bypass under a natural configuration (Section III).

V-B Adding a trusted entity

We now add a trusted entity 𝒯\mathcal{T}, which can keep secret state and perform cryptographic operations, and ask which channels between 𝒯\mathcal{T} and the other parties are necessary for a secure protocol to be constructed. Although Basin et al. [13] also consider topologies containing a trusted entity, they operate in a restricted setting where 𝒯\mathcal{T}’s channels are either secure or insecure, therefore their model is unable to distinguish between different types of trusted device and the resulting channels, as we do here and in Section VI-C.

A trusted entity enables the construction of a secure I-HITL only if the adversary cannot stand in for it. If the adversary can read everything 𝒯\mathcal{T} receives from 𝒮\mathcal{S} and inject on every channel from 𝒯\mathcal{T} to 𝒮\mathcal{S}, it can run a copy of 𝒯\mathcal{T} in its place, and 𝒮\mathcal{S} ends up with verification material generated by the adversary, exactly as in Theorem 4.

Proposition 5 (Necessary channels).

Let τ\tau be a topology of Figure 4 and Σ\Sigma a complete I-HITL protocol for (ℳ,τ)(\mathcal{M}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\tau), where ℋ\mathcal{H} is not restricted to programs in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. If

  1. (i)

    ℓ𝒯​ℋ∈{∅,𝗂𝗇𝗌,𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁}\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}}\in\{\varnothing\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{auth}\} and ℓℋ​𝒯∈{∅,𝗂𝗇𝗌,𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿}\ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}}\in\{\varnothing\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{conf}\}, or

  2. (ii)

    ℓ𝒮​𝒯∈{∅,𝗂𝗇𝗌,𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁}\ell_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}}\in\{\varnothing\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{auth}\} and ℓ𝒯​𝒮∈{∅,𝗂𝗇𝗌,𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿}\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{S}}\in\{\varnothing\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{conf}\},

then Σ\Sigma is not approval-binding.

The proof is given in Appendix A. By Proposition 5, a trusted entity can be useful for ℋ\mathcal{H} in exactly two ways: by showing ℋ\mathcal{H} something the adversary cannot read (ℓ𝒯​ℋ∈{𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿,𝗌𝖾𝖼}\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}}\in\{\mathsf{conf}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{sec}\}) or by receiving from ℋ\mathcal{H} something the adversary cannot forge (ℓℋ​𝒯∈{𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁,𝗌𝖾𝖼}\ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}}\in\{\mathsf{auth}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{sec}\}), and for the service in the two analogous ways. We now prove that these capabilities suffice for I-HITL. Our constructions for the proof use a signature scheme (𝖪𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝖵𝖾𝗋)(\mathsf{KGen}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{Sign}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{SigVer}), modeled symbolically as discussed in Section IV, and only require that ℋ\mathcal{H} can run programs in 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Proposition 6 (Sufficient channels).

Let τ\tau be a topology of Figure 4 with

  1. (i)

    ℓ𝒯​ℋ∈{𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿,𝗌𝖾𝖼}\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}}\in\{\mathsf{conf}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{sec}\} or ℓℋ​𝒯∈{𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁,𝗌𝖾𝖼}\ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}}\in\{\mathsf{auth}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{sec}\}, and

  2. (ii)

    ℓ𝒮​𝒯∈{𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿,𝗌𝖾𝖼}\ell_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}}\in\{\mathsf{conf}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{sec}\} or ℓ𝒯​𝒮∈{𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁,𝗌𝖾𝖼}\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{S}}\in\{\mathsf{auth}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{sec}\}.

Then there is a complete, approval-binding I-HITL protocol for (ℳ,τ)(\mathcal{M}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\tau).

Figure 5 gives the constructed protocols for each case: one enrollment protocol per alternative of (ii) and one approval protocol per alternative of (i), any pairing of which is a secure I-HITL protocol for τ\tau. In all of them 𝒯\mathcal{T} holds a signing key, proofs are signatures, and 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒:=𝖲𝗂𝗀𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Verify}:=\mathsf{SigVer}. The proof is given in Appendix A. Both propositions together completely characterize secure I-HITL protocols:

Theorem 7.

For a topology τ\tau of Figure 4, there is a complete, approval-binding I-HITL protocol for (ℳ,τ)(\mathcal{M}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\tau) if and only if

  1. (i)

    ℓ𝒯​ℋ∈{𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿,𝗌𝖾𝖼}\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}}\in\{\mathsf{conf}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{sec}\} or ℓℋ​𝒯∈{𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁,𝗌𝖾𝖼}\ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}}\in\{\mathsf{auth}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{sec}\}, and

  2. (ii)

    ℓ𝒮​𝒯∈{𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿,𝗌𝖾𝖼}\ell_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}}\in\{\mathsf{conf}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{sec}\} or ℓ𝒯​𝒮∈{𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁,𝗌𝖾𝖼}\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{S}}\in\{\mathsf{auth}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{sec}\}.

Theorem 7 says nothing about where the labels on each 𝒯\mathcal{T} channel come from in the first place. A trusted entity’s channels are determined by the device that realizes it and by the human’s behavior when interacting with that device. The next section explores these factors in practice, deriving channel labels from device characteristics such as whether 𝒯\mathcal{T}’s key is attested or extractable, and whether an adversarial human attempts to delegate to the agent. The theorem then lets us characterize which approaches allow I-HITL protocols.

VI Realizing Channels in Practice

Many approaches used for authentication (hardware wallets, authenticator apps, etc.) appear well-suited to realizing I-HITL, but the analysis in preceding sections shows achieving approval-binding can be subtle. In this section we explore whether I-HITL can be realized by devices and protocols in use today. We focus on standalone hardware devices and mobile phone-based authentication protocols, disregarding some possible instantiations of 𝒯\mathcal{T} such as in-person interaction. Section VI-A derives labels on 𝒯↔𝒮\mathcal{T}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{S} channels (ℓ𝒮​𝒯,ℓ𝒯​𝒮)(\ell_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{S}}) based on a trusted entity’s key management. Section VI-B similarly explains how the display and user inputs provided by a trusted entity determine the labels of ℋ↔𝒯\mathcal{H}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{T} channels (ℓℋ​𝒯,ℓ𝒯​ℋ)(\ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}}). Section VI-C applies the analysis in the preceding subsections to specific authentication methods in use today, and using Theorem 7, classifies them according to their ability to realize I-HITL.

Theorem 7 is stated in terms of channel labels, but these labels are not directly observable to the verifier of an I-HITL proof (whether this is the service itself or an external verifier). Throughout this section we therefore work in terms of the strongest channel labels which can be confirmed by a verifier. For instance, if a device serving as 𝒯\mathcal{T} has a display which lets it realize a secure channel to ℋ\mathcal{H}, but it generates no evidence which can be used to verify the existence of this channel, we treat the channel as insecure.

VI-A 𝒯↔𝒮\mathcal{T}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{S} channel labels

In practice, the labels between 𝒯\mathcal{T} and 𝒮\mathcal{S} depend upon a secret key kk held by 𝒯\mathcal{T} but not the adversary. We write kk to distinguish it from the signing key 𝗌𝗄{\sf sk} of the I-HITL protocol constructions, though in practice the two may coincide. Since initially all channels between the two are insecure, establishing a new channel requires two properties of kk: it must be bound, i.e., verifiably held by 𝒯\mathcal{T} rather than by a party impersonating it, and it must be isolated, i.e., not held by any adversarial party. Neither property is directly observable by a verifier. Both instead rest on attestation: evidence, verifiable against a root of trust, that kk was generated within 𝒯\mathcal{T} and whether it is extractable by ℋ\mathcal{H}. Attestation settles binding outright, but settles isolation only if kk is not extractable, otherwise isolation, and therefore the channel labels, depend on whether ℋ\mathcal{H} acts honestly or adversarially—a feature of our threat model that differs critically from previous models of human principals [34, 72, 15, 14, 84, 33].

Key attestation (attested / unattested):  Some devices, e.g., Yubikeys [90] and Ledger wallets [47], can digitally sign the keys they generate, where signatures are verifiable against a manufacturer root of trust. Mobile phones generally provide an analogous capability, verifiable against the OS vendor’s root, which installed apps may optionally use to provide evidence of their key management. We use the designation attested for such devices. Other trusted hardware devices, e.g., standard crypto wallets, lack this capability and are unattested, so is any key that 𝒯\mathcal{T} did not generate, such as a shared secret delivered by 𝒮\mathcal{S}, since attestation can only speak to keys created within 𝒯\mathcal{T}. When a device is attested, 𝒮\mathcal{S} can use an attestation to verify that key kk is truly held by 𝒯\mathcal{T} and subject to a fixed policy. Without attestation, 𝒮\mathcal{S} cannot tell whether kk is held by the adversary, so both channel labels are ins.

Key control (extractable / encumbered):  Even if a key generated by a device is attested, it may still be extractable by the user. This is in fact an important feature in systems that do not support key rotation, e.g., cryptocurrency addresses. Keys that are not extractable by a user are referred to as encumbered [41]. Key control is a property of the device’s policy reported by attestation, so 𝒮\mathcal{S} can verify whether kk is encumbered. A device may hold both extractable and encumbered keys.

Trust model for ℋ\mathcal{H} (honest / delegating):  An honest ℋ\mathcal{H} does not attempt to delegate control to an agent, and therefore can be trusted to not extract and share the device key kk, even if extraction is possible. However a delegating ℋ\mathcal{H} may do so in order to allow an agent to communicate with 𝒮\mathcal{S} and bypass a HITL gate. If ℋ\mathcal{H} is assumed to be honest, then any attestation suffices as evidence that key kk is held only by 𝒯\mathcal{T}, and can be used to establish an authentic channel to 𝒮\mathcal{S} (if kk signs messages) or a confidential channel from 𝒮\mathcal{S} (if kk is the private half of an encryption key pair). However, if ℋ\mathcal{H} attempts to delegate, 𝒮\mathcal{S} cannot know whether kk is held by the adversary unless the attestation also proves that kk is encumbered.

Table I summarizes the channel labels each combination of key properties establishes under either assumption on ℋ\mathcal{H}.

VI-B ℋ↔𝒯\mathcal{H}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{T} channel labels

The labels between 𝒯\mathcal{T} and ℋ\mathcal{H} are determined by 𝒯\mathcal{T}’s two human-facing interfaces: a display, through which it sends requests, and a user input, through which ℋ\mathcal{H} can respond. The properties of the display and user input determine the labels as follows:

Display trust (trusted / untrusted):  A display is trusted if the adversary cannot show the human a request that appears to come from 𝒯\mathcal{T}, by overlay or imitation. Examples include a hardware wallet’s screen and TEE-rendered UIs [5]. A display on a phone may also be trusted if the identity of the app controlling it is known, the app enforces suitable protections, and the integrity of the OS can be verified. It is untrusted otherwise, e.g., a browser tab or app running on an untrusted platform, which the agent can replicate pixel for pixel [16], or SMS and email, whose sender IDs are easily spoofed. A trusted display realizes an authentic channel from 𝒯\mathcal{T} to ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Display privacy (private / exposed):  A display is private if the adversary cannot read it and exposed if it can: a private display realizes a confidential channel from 𝒯\mathcal{T} to ℋ\mathcal{H}. Private displays include the screens of devices the agent does not control, such as an external hardware wallet. A phone screen, by contrast, is potentially exposed even without OS compromise as accessibility services, which phone agents commonly use to operate other apps, can read the content of any app’s window [4].

User input trust (trusted / untrusted):  A user input is trusted if the adversary can neither operate nor simulate it. A keyboard or touchscreen to an agent-controlled device is untrusted, because the same accessibility API that exposes the screen also lets an app perform taps, gestures, and text entry [4]. A trusted user input therefore typically relies on hardware that software cannot drive, e.g., the buttons of a hardware wallet, the touchscreen of a Ledger Stax or Flex, which the secure element controls directly, or a phone’s side button and biometric sensor, whose input is delivered to secure hardware rather than to the OS. A trusted user input instantiates an auth channel from the human to 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

User input action (keypad / confirmation):  We refer to an user input as a keypad if a human can send arbitrary messages on it and a confirmation if it conveys one bit per request, such as a button. A trusted keypad instantiates an auth channel from ℋ\mathcal{H} to 𝒯\mathcal{T}. A trusted confirmation only allows a single authentic bit to be communicated: 𝒯\mathcal{T} displays the message it is about to sign and signs it when the human presses the button, so the press says that the human agreed, not to which message. If the display is untrusted, the adversary can show the human a benign m′m^{\prime} in place of mm, and the human’s genuine press approves mm, yielding an ins channel from ℋ\mathcal{H} to 𝒯\mathcal{T}. With a trusted display, the human sees the mm that 𝒯\mathcal{T} signs, and the confirmation and display together realize an auth channel from ℋ\mathcal{H} to 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Table II summarizes the labels established by each combination of display and input.

VI-C Devices and I-HITL

We now consider concrete instantiations of 𝒯\mathcal{T}, exploring both standalone trusted devices and mobile applications. For each we analyze the properties of its display, its input, and its key management. Together with Table I and Table II, these properties determine the labels on 𝒯\mathcal{T}’s channels, and hence, by Theorem 7, whether the approach realizes I-HITL. Table III summarizes our findings, the full analysis is deferred to Appendix E.

We evaluate each instantiation under our two trust models for ℋ\mathcal{H}, honest and delegating. If an instantiation is secure under a delegating ℋ\mathcal{H} we say it realizes strong I-HITL, if it is secure only under an honest ℋ\mathcal{H} it realizes weak I-HITL. The distinction is relevant because in some settings a service needs assurance that ℋ\mathcal{H} approved an action, even when they may not trust ℋ\mathcal{H}. Under weak I-HITL a delegating ℋ\mathcal{H} can hand the agent the means to approve on its behalf, and the service cannot distinguish the agent’s approvals from the human’s. A proof π\pi therefore establishes nothing about who approved, and ℋ\mathcal{H} can disavow any action by attributing it to the agent. Under strong I-HITL no such delegation is possible, and π\pi can serve as the evidence that the human, not the agent, approved the action. A delegating ℋ\mathcal{H} may still approve without inspection, but cannot falsely claim that their approval was hijacked by an adversarial agent to avoid being held responsible.

The two Ledger configurations in Table III run on the same hardware and differ only in key management: a key derived from the user’s recovery seed is attested but extractable, since the user holds the seed by design, and so realizes only weak I-HITL. Encumbrance is thus a property of how 𝒯\mathcal{T} manages kk, not of the device alone.

Table III is not exhaustive, but apart from our construction the three standalone devices listed are the only instantiations of I-HITL we found. Of the instantiations that realize strong I-HITL, all except ours require dedicated hardware. The Wultra Talisman is issued by banks and enterprises to their own customers, and Ledger wallets are purchased and carried for specific applications (e.g., cryptocurrency management). Realizing I-HITL on a Ledger device also requires a purpose-built app, since the endorsement keys are issued per application. Thus the Ledger rows of Table III reflect what the hardware can support, not what shipped Ledger apps currently provide. Our construction relies only on the attestation and key management capabilities available to any Android or iOS application, so it may be deployed without requiring users to acquire new devices.

VII Countersign

In this section, we present Countersign, a mobile phone-based strong I-HITL implementation. Mobile phones are a natural candidate for 𝒯\mathcal{T} because they have the necessary interfaces and attestation capabilities, and are readily accessible to users. Yet, as shown by in Section VI, many mobile phone applications providing closely related functionality (e.g., authentication and proof of personhood) fail to realize strong I-HITL. Countersign demonstrates that the necessary capabilities for I-HITL exist on mobile phones (under reasonable assumptions), and many similar applications are insecure simply because their workflow is designed for a subtly different threat model. Countersign’s core I-HITL logic consists of ∼\sim800 LOC for the backend service, and ∼\sim150 LOC each for the Android/iOS application (excluding generic scaffolding such as configuration, data models, and user interfaces), illustrating the feasibility of achieving I-HITL in practice. Our code is open-source at https://github.com/I-HITL/countersign, low-level implementation details are deferred to Appendix F.

VII-A Mobile Phone Attestation Capabilities

In our instantiation, the trusted entity 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a mobile application running on a commodity phone, so we rely on the phone to execute the application faithfully and to manage its keys securely. Our design leverages the attestation mechanisms provided by the Android and iOS ecosystems to allow 𝒮\mathcal{S} to verify the security properties of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. 𝒮\mathcal{S} must establish two properties. The first is code integrity: the application handling requests and controlling the device must be an honest implementation, running on an operating system that has not been tampered with (i.e., rooted or jailbroken). The second is key management: the verification key 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk} must be generated and stored in secure hardware, with any exportability and usage restrictions enforced by that hardware, as characterized in Section VI-A. We examine here how the Android and iOS attestation mechanisms support these requirements.

Android.  To verify app integrity, Android applications can make requests to the Play Integrity API [38], which returns a Google-signed verdict with two key fields. First, the device verdict states whether the device is a certified Android device with a locked bootloader, an unmodified system image, and recent security patches. Second, the app verdict states whether the app on the device matches the binary distributed through Google Play. Regarding key management, apps can generate and use keys through the Android Keystore system [36]. An app that generates a hardware-backed key using the keystore (backed by either a TEE on the main processor, or a dedicated hardware component called the StrongBox) can request an attestation certificate chain for that key. The leaf certificate chains to Google’s root of trust, and contains an extension specifying the attested key’s security properties, including whether it resides in the TEE or StrongBox (and therefore cannot be exported), its permitted uses, whether each use requires user authentication and by what method, and the identity of the app that generated it.

iOS.  To verify app integrity, iOS applications can make requests to the App Attest service [9], which returns an Apple-signed attestation that a service can use to verify that the request came from a genuine instance of the app, as Apple distributed it, on a genuine Apple device. Unlike Play Integrity, however, the attestation makes no statement about the integrity of the operating system itself, so a service relying on it must additionally assume that the device is not jailbroken, an assumption it cannot verify. Regarding key management, apps can generate key pairs whose private key is stored in a dedicated hardware component, the Secure Enclave, from which it cannot be exported. The same App Attest attestation certifies this property for a key and names the app that generated it, so a service learns both that the key is hardware-held and which genuine app holds it. Subsequently, the app can sign requests to its server with the key, in a format fixed by App Attest that adds a counter for replay protection. Unlike an Android keystore key, however, the key’s use cannot be made conditional on user authentication such as Face ID.

VII-B Realizing I-HITL Channels in Countersign

Figure 6 depicts the topology of Countersign and the features of the mobile device used to realize 𝒯\mathcal{T}’s channel labels. With channels established, Countersign uses the enroll-by-authenticated-key, approve-by-message construction given in Figure 5. Here we explain each channel label in more detail. The header of each paragraph specifies the channel label we consider, the mechanism used to protect that channel, and the formal label in ℒ\mathcal{L} we argue is realized by our implementation.

ℓ𝒯​ℋ\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}}: Trusted display, auth.  A phone has no display that software cannot drive, so Countersign relies on device/code integrity to ensure the agent cannot show ℋ\mathcal{H} a false request. The approval screen is drawn by the Countersign binary, and 𝒮\mathcal{S} has verified through attestation that this binary is genuine and running on an unmodified OS. Given an honest OS, the remaining attack is overlay: an agent-controlled app draws over the approval screen. Countersign defends against this on Android by rendering the approval screen with overlays blocked and checking at approval-time that its own window holds focus and is unobscured; iOS does not permit cross-app overlays at all. The display remains exposed in the sense of Table II and does not provide confidentiality (for instance, accessibility services could read the contents of the approval screen) and therefore the channel is auth but not sec.

ℓℋ​𝒯\ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}}: Biometric input, auth.  The input interface of Countersign allows confirmation in the sense of Section VI-B: ℋ\mathcal{H} conveys one bit per request, by presenting a biometric. As the biometric sensor delivers its reading to secure hardware rather than to the app or OS, the agent can not simulate it from software. By Table II, a trusted confirmation yields an auth channel only together with the trusted display described in the previous paragraph. On Android, the signing key is generated with a per-use biometric requirement enforced by the keystore, and attested to by the key’s certificate. On iOS, the App Attest key cannot enforce such a biometric policy on a hardware level, so Countersign uses a second Secure Enclave (which is not App Attest) key whose public key is signed by the App Attest key, and which does have a per-use biometric requirement. This means that on Android the biometric requirement is attested through hardware, while on iOS it is a claim by the attested app, and holds only as long as code integrity holds. In both cases, the binding of the biometric to the message seen by ℋ\mathcal{H} requires code integrity, since on Android the hardware learns that a biometric succeeded but not what was on screen.

ℓ𝒯​𝒮\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{S}}: Remote attestation, auth.  Countersign sends 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk} to 𝒮\mathcal{S} together with attestation evidence, bound to a challenge issued by 𝒮\mathcal{S}. On Android, the evidence consists of the key attestation and a Play Integrity token whose nonce commits to the same service challenge. 𝒮\mathcal{S} verifies the key attestation chain to Google’s root, checks that the key is hardware-backed, gated by device authentication, and was created by the correct app, and separately checks that the integrity verdict recognizes the binary, the signing certificate, and the device. On iOS, 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk} is a Secure Enclave key generated alongside a separate App Attest key. 𝒮\mathcal{S} verifies the App Attest key’s attestation to Apple’s root, then uses that key to verify a signature over 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk}. In either case, 𝒮\mathcal{S} learns that 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk} belongs to an attested instance of Countersign, placing Countersign in the encumbered, attested row of Table I. This establishes an auth channel from 𝒯\mathcal{T} to 𝒮\mathcal{S} under both honest and delegating humans, allowing Countersign to realize strong I-HITL.

ℓ𝒮​𝒯\ell_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}}: ins.  The channel ℓ𝒮​𝒯\ell_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}} is not used by Countersign, and can be considered insecure for our purposes.

Comparison to existing apps.  The mechanisms described above are available to any mobile app, and push authenticators (e.g., Duo Mobile, Microsoft Authenticator, Okta Verify) already use several of them, but still fall short of I-HITL due to issues in their workflow. First, attestation of ℓ𝒯​𝒮\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{S}} is only beginning to appear: Duo Mobile on Android now appears to use attestation, but this is undocumented and unevenly enforced, and third-party clients have historically been able to enroll in place of a genuine app [1]. Second, the approval is not bound to the message ℋ\mathcal{H} sees but instead an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-selected identifier, so 𝒮\mathcal{S} is not left with a publicly verifiable proof of approval for accountability purposes. Third, ℓℋ​𝒯\ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}} typically uses the touchscreen as an input interface, which in contrast to hardware-backed biometrics is simulatable in software. Finally, these apps often fall back to alternate methods of approval such as exportable passcode seeds, SMS messages, and backup-based re-enrollment. These fallbacks may be acceptable for pure authentication, where the human is trusted and recoverability is an important feature, but compromise I-HITL.

VII-C Limitations

In this section we discuss limitations surfaced by our implementation: device capabilities or ecosystem characteristics which require additional trust assumptions. These gaps could be filled by future development of mobile devices to allow stronger I-HITL guarantees.

Trusted display.  On both Android and iOS the Countersign app relies on the OS to prevent other applications from tampering with the approval screen, and to bind the displayed message to the trusted confirmation. A more robust implementation would remove this dependency. Android Protected Confirmation (APC) [37] previously provided a path to exactly this: a TEE rendered the prompt and signed the message together with a hash of what it displayed, so the display was trusted and the confirmation bound to the message without any trust in the OS. However, APC was deprecated due to low adoption and high maintenance costs [37]. Its return, or an equivalent on iOS, would let Countersign realize ℓ𝒯​ℋ\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}} as a trusted display without relying on OS integrity.

Device integrity on iOS.  On Android, the Play Integrity API [38] provides evidence of device integrity which does not have an equivalent on iOS. In particular, the service cannot determine from App Attest whether the device has been jailbroken. Additionally, while iOS supports biometric authentication, App Attest keys cannot be configured to require biometric authentication before use. Instead, this restriction must be enforced by the app, whose integrity may not be preserved on a compromised OS. On Android, by contrast, the per-use biometric requirement is enforced by the secure hardware and reported in the key’s attestation, so the service need not trust the application for it. Consequently, our iOS implementation relies on the additional assumption that the operating system remains trustworthy to enforce the integrity of biometric authentication.

Roots of trust.  Every channel label in Section VII-B ultimately rests on a certificate chain to Google’s or Apple’s root. This is a stronger trust assumption than the manufacturer root of a hardware wallet, which is used only at provisioning. Apple/Google’s servers must be reachable to issue attestations, so an outage blocks enrollment. The evidence provided by attestation is also is a snapshot of device/application state at the moment of verification rather than an enduring guarantee. A key attestation certificate records the verified-boot state at key generation, and an App Attest attestation is issued once, so neither is invalidated by a kernel compromise after enrollment. On Android, Countersign narrows this window by requesting a fresh Play Integrity verdict with every approval. However, this cannot detect if a kernel is compromised after boot, since verified boot measures the system only at boot. The effective window on Android is therefore the interval since the last boot. On iOS there is no corresponding mechanism, and the window is the interval since enrollment.

Key recovery.  We do not address the issue of key recovery for 𝒯\mathcal{T} in our initial implementation of Countersign. As strong I-HITL requires that ℋ\mathcal{H} cannot directly access 𝗌𝗄{\sf sk}, any recovery path will require ℋ\mathcal{H} to re-execute a procedure like 𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅\mathsf{Enroll} in order to restore an encrypted copy of 𝗌𝗄{\sf sk} kept by a trusted entity such as 𝒮\mathcal{S} or to generate a fresh 𝗌𝗄{\sf sk}.

VIII Related work

HITL and permissions in agent systems:  HITL approval is a standard recommendation for agent control [74] and a common feature of agent frameworks; Michael and Roesner [58] survey such permission mechanisms and note the absence of formally verified enforcement. Work on agent policy, e.g., [30, 75, 83], specifies which actions an agent may take, and complements our focus on securely enforcing those human approvals dictated by policy.

User authentication:  User authentication, including a long line of work on 2FA (e.g., [19]), considers how to verify the identity of a particular user, but assumes a trusted client device. (Otherwise, session hijacking is fatal.) Formal analyses of FIDO2, for instance, exclude compromised clients from their guarantees and model user approval as a one-bit gesture [12, 17]. An agent, however, can compromise both 2FA factors when they converge on a host [31, 43], and effectively hijack an authenticated session. Hardware-based transaction authentication, e.g., using hardware wallets [10], arose for exactly this reason, although, as Table III shows, they are not always sufficient for I-HITL. I-HITL can be viewed as a generalization of transaction authentication to agent systems, where transactions can be of many different types and where adversarial delegation poses a concern.

Agent authorization:  A number of works on AI agents (e.g., [76]) and standards specifications (e.g., MCP [60]) consider ways of using existing authorization infrastructure, such as OAuth, to authorize agents. These rely on existing user authentication, and where they call for human approval of an action, they leave unspecified how that approval reaches the service. When the human reaches the identity provider or approval prompt through the agent’s platform, these designs fall in the plain topology of Theorem 4.

Approved vs. executed actions:  Classical work on authorization from untrusted terminals [2, 11, 3] shows the danger of signed approvals in the face of a deceptive rendering layer (a problem sometimes called what you see is what you sign (WYSIWYS)). Weng [85] adapts WYSIWYS to agent approvals, but simply assumes a trusted path. Transaction-authentication devices [84] and trusted-path systems [91] address the issues in these works by giving the human a channel that bypasses a potentially compromised host. Our trusted entity TT plays a similar role, but we characterize exactly which channels TT needs and, unlike classical schemes, consider adversarial human delegation. Relatedly, Loopjacking [44] studies the failure in which an implementation applies a genuine approval of one operation to a different one. Approval binding rules this out at the gate, since a proof verifies only for the message the human approved. We assume the service then executes that message faithfully [92].

Proof of Personhood (PoP): Many proposed [20] and deployed systems aim to enable online services to distinguish humans and bots. The best known, World, issues a credential to a human whose uniqueness is established biometrically or using a national identity document. World’s human-in-the-loop package [80] gates agent actions on a World ID proof, but does not realize I-HITL, for two reasons. (1) The human never sees the action on a trusted display: the action is rendered only by the agent’s platform, and the World app displays a description that the platform also supplies and that is bound neither to the proof nor to the service’s signature on the request. (2) The documented integration exposes approval as a tool that the agent chooses whether to invoke, unless the developer separately verifies the proof before the protected action executes, as World’s documentation now advises [87], the agent can bypass the gate by not invoking it. An unreleased revision of the package replaces World ID proofs with a standard World ID login, which never shows the human the action. The approval it produces is checked with a secret stored on the same server that runs the agent, so a compromised platform can forge it. More broadly, World does not aim to prevent delegation: AgentKit [86] links agent wallets to verified humans. Additionally, because World aims to deduplicate humans, it requires use of a single global registry, greatly limiting its scope of application.22 2 Users from only 17 countries are currently eligible for identity-document-based authentication.

Other notions of PoP, e.g., [47], give assurance of human approval only to the user herself, not a relying service.

Secure human–server communication:  Building on security ceremonies [34, 72], Basin et al. [13] characterize the topologies permitting authentic or confidential human–server communication through a compromised platform. We adopt their topology framework and impossibility argument, but differ in key ways: they fix all non-platform channels as secure and let the device share keys with the server a priori, whereas we grade each trusted-entity channel independently and assume no initial knowledge, making key establishment (and hence attestation and encumbrance) central to our characterization (Theorem 7). Our goal also differs from theirs, in that we bind a human’s approval to an adversary-chosen message through a publicly verifiable proof, including (for strong I-HITL) against a human who attempts to delegate approval to the agent.

IX Conclusion

HITL gates are widely deployed as a critical line of defense against misbehaving agents, yet most operate in a topology that does not separate the agent from the resources used to approve its actions. Our experiments with a mainstream agentic wallet show the practical consequences. Given access to the inbox that receives a gate’s OTPs and a task blocked by a spending cap, most frontier models will autonomously bypass the gate. Some will do so on an attacker’s instruction and send the attacker money.

We introduced I-HITL to formalize what a secure HITL gate must guarantee, and strong I-HITL to extend that guarantee to humans who attempt to delegate approvals to agents in violation of oversight policies. In a symbolic model of channel security we proved that a trusted entity is necessary for I-HITL (Theorem 4) but not sufficient (Theorem 7): this entity must attest to the keys it generates and, for strong I-HITL, encumber them. We classified existing devices against these requirements and presented Countersign, which realizes strong I-HITL on off-the-shelf Android and iOS devices.

Takeaways for deployers and platform vendors.  The default topology of many agentic systems, in which the gate co-resides with the agent, fails in principle (Theorem 4) and in practice (Section III). Guidance that restricts agent capabilities (e.g., denying email access) shifts the burden to users and is unlikely to hold; we urge service vendors to adopt the stronger assurances I-HITL makes achievable. We likewise urge authenticator-app vendors to offer an I-HITL approval mode, since push authenticators already implement most of the required mechanisms (Section VII-B). We finally urge mobile OS vendors to supply two missing primitives: a TEE-rendered confirmation UI and attestable gating of key use on biometric authentication.

Takeaway for regulators.  Regulations such as the EU AI Act [35] mandate human oversight without specifying how to define or evidence it. Strong I-HITL offers a conceptual springboard for regulatory frameworks and, in systems such as Countersign, a mechanism for producing verifiable evidence of compliance in the form of human approval (although not evidence of due attention).

Open problems.  On the analytic side, a computational treatment would give finer-grained guarantees than our symbolic one. On the practical side, the key question is how to extend I-HITL beyond end-user platforms to enterprise systems and, critically, to the infrastructure on which frontier models themselves run, where an agent may be positioned to gate its own oversight (Example 2). By Theorem 4, such work would begin by establishing a local service 𝒮\mathcal{S} isolated from the agent, e.g., in a hardware enclave, with a trusted entity 𝒯\mathcal{T} likewise outside the agent’s reach.
