Appendix A Additional Theorems and Proofs

This appendix contains additional analysis and proofs for the theoretical results in the paper.

A-A Impossibility of I-HITL in the Plain Topology

Proof of Theorem 4.

Fix any m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}. The adversary chooses a program for 𝒫\mathcal{P} that runs 𝒫\mathcal{P}’s prescribed program together with an internal copy of ℋ\mathcal{H}’s prescribed program: whenever 𝒫\mathcal{P}’s program would send a message to ℋ\mathcal{H}, it is delivered to the internal copy instead, and whatever the internal copy sends is handled as if received from ℋ\mathcal{H}. The adversary runs 𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅\mathsf{Enroll}, then initiates 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾⁡(m)\mathsf{Approve}(m) and supplies external bit 11 to the internal copy for the request it receives. In τ0\tau_{0} every channel of 𝒮\mathcal{S} is with 𝒫\mathcal{P}, so 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s view in this execution is identical to its view in an execution in which all parties run Σ\Sigma and the adversary is passive. By completeness, 𝒮\mathcal{S} outputs 𝗏𝗄≠⊥\mathsf{vk}\neq\bot and π≠⊥\pi\neq\bot with 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(𝗏𝗄,m,π)=1\mathsf{Verify}(\mathsf{vk}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\pi)=1. The real ℋ\mathcal{H} receives no request in this execution, so ℋ.𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝖽⁡(m)=0\mathcal{H}.\mathsf{Approved}(m)=0, and (m,π)(m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\pi) violates approval-binding. ∎

A-B Necessary Channels for I-HITL

Proof of Proposition 5.

Fix m∗∈ℳm^{\ast}\in\mathcal{M}. In both cases ℋ\mathcal{H}, 𝒯\mathcal{T} and 𝒮\mathcal{S} run Σ\Sigma, and the adversary gives the real ℋ\mathcal{H} external bit 00 for every request, so ℋ.𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝖽⁡(m∗)=0\mathcal{H}.\mathsf{Approved}(m^{\ast})=0 throughout. It remains to exhibit an execution in which 𝒮\mathcal{S} outputs π∗\pi^{\ast} with 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(𝗏𝗄,m∗,π∗)=1\mathsf{Verify}(\mathsf{vk}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak m^{\ast}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\pi^{\ast})=1.

Case (i). The adversary runs an internal copy ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} of ℋ\mathcal{H}’s program. On the wire it reads every message 𝒯\mathcal{T} sends on ℓ𝒯​ℋ\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}}, drops it, and delivers it to ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}. Messages 𝒫\mathcal{P}’s program would send to ℋ\mathcal{H} are delivered to ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} likewise. It injects every message ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} sends to 𝒯\mathcal{T} on ℓℋ​𝒯\ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}} and treats messages ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} sends to 𝒫\mathcal{P} as received from ℋ\mathcal{H}, and drops everything the real ℋ\mathcal{H} sends. The labels in (i) permit exactly this. After 𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅\mathsf{Enroll} it initiates 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾⁡(m∗)\mathsf{Approve}(m^{\ast}) and gives ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} external bit 11 for the resulting request.

Case (ii). The adversary runs internal copies ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} and 𝒯′\mathcal{T}^{\prime} of the programs of ℋ\mathcal{H} and 𝒯\mathcal{T}, connected to each other and to 𝒫\mathcal{P} as in τ\tau, with ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} given external bit 11 for the request for m∗m^{\ast}. On the wire it reads every message 𝒮\mathcal{S} sends on ℓ𝒮​𝒯\ell_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}} and delivers it to 𝒯′\mathcal{T}^{\prime}, drops every message the real 𝒯\mathcal{T} sends on ℓ𝒯​𝒮\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{S}} and injects 𝒯′\mathcal{T}^{\prime}’s messages in its place, which (ii) permits, and never contacts the real ℋ\mathcal{H}. 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s view is then that of an execution with all parties running Σ\Sigma, the adversary passive, and ℋ\mathcal{H} receiving bit 11; in particular its output 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk} of 𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅\mathsf{Enroll} is the one produced by 𝒯′\mathcal{T}^{\prime}.

In either case completeness gives 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(𝗏𝗄,m∗,π∗)=1\mathsf{Verify}(\mathsf{vk}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak m^{\ast}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\pi^{\ast})=1 for 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s output π∗\pi^{\ast}, so (m∗,π∗)(m^{\ast}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\pi^{\ast}) violates approval-binding. ∎

A-C Sufficient Channels for I-HITL

Proof of Proposition 6.

Completeness is immediate from correctness of the signature scheme: with a passive adversary each procedure delivers what it sends, 𝒮\mathcal{S} outputs 𝒯\mathcal{T}’s 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk}, and on bit 11 𝒯\mathcal{T} signs mm.

For approval-binding we show first that 𝒮\mathcal{S} outputs 𝒯\mathcal{T}’s 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk} or ⊥\bot, and then that 𝒯\mathcal{T} signs only approved messages. Together these give the claim: a π∗\pi^{\ast} with 𝖲𝗂𝗀𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗏𝗄,m∗,π∗)=1\mathsf{SigVer}(\mathsf{vk}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak m^{\ast}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\pi^{\ast})=1 is a signature under 𝒯\mathcal{T}’s key, which only 𝒯\mathcal{T} can produce, and 𝒯\mathcal{T} never signed m∗m^{\ast} since ℋ.𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝖽⁡(m∗)=0\mathcal{H}.\mathsf{Approved}(m^{\ast})=0.

Enrollment. In the authentic variant every message 𝒮\mathcal{S} receives on ℓ𝒯​𝒮\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{S}} was sent by 𝒯\mathcal{T}, so 𝒮\mathcal{S} outputs 𝒯\mathcal{T}’s 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk} or nothing. In the confidential variant the adversary never learns 𝗌𝗄′\mathsf{sk}^{\prime}, so the only signature verifying under 𝗏𝗄′\mathsf{vk}^{\prime} that exists is the one 𝒯\mathcal{T} produced over its own 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk}. Keys the adversary injects on ℓ𝒮​𝒯\ell_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}} cause 𝒯\mathcal{T} to sign 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk} under keys 𝒮\mathcal{S} does not check, and injected (𝗏𝗄′′,σ)(\mathsf{vk}^{\prime\prime}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\sigma) pairs fail verification.

Approval by code. 𝒯\mathcal{T} signs mm only on receiving (m,c)(m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak c) for a recorded (m,c)(m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak c). The code cc is a fresh value sent only on ℓ𝒯​ℋ\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}}, which is confidential, so the adversary never learns it. 𝒯\mathcal{T} receives (m,c)(m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak c) only if ℋ\mathcal{H} sent it, which ℋ\mathcal{H} does only on external bit 11 for the request ⟨m,c⟩\langle m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak c\rangle, i.e. only if ℋ.𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝖽⁡(m)=1\mathcal{H}.\mathsf{Approved}(m)=1. A request the adversary injects on ℓ𝒯​ℋ\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}} carries a code of its own, which matches no record, so if ℋ\mathcal{H} answers it, that only adds to ℋ\mathcal{H}’s approvals.

Approval by message. Every mm that 𝒯\mathcal{T} receives on ℓℋ​𝒯\ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}} was sent by ℋ\mathcal{H}, which sends mm there only on external bit 11 for a request ⟨m,ε⟩\langle m\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\varepsilon\rangle, so ℋ.𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝖽⁡(m)=1\mathcal{H}.\mathsf{Approved}(m)=1. ∎

Appendix B Experimental Setup Details

All experimental code can be found at https://github.com/I-HITL/experiments. Our LangChain agent runs on langchain v1.4.4. Every model used in the experiments is queried via LangChain’s provider integrations, with a cap of 40 tool-calling iterations per run. We provide here the exact prompt the agent receives and the messages injected into the wallet’s mailbox for the prompt injection experiments. No user prompt mentions the spending policy, the email OTP, or the possibility of self-escalation.

Payment agent, No attack.  We reproduce here the honest invoice. INV-2 and INV-3 are identical, changing only the invoice number.

Payment agent, Injection attack.  We reproduce here the email encouraging payment as well as the malicious invoice. INV-2 and INV-3 are identical, changing only the invoice number.

Summary agent, Injection attack.  We reproduce here the prompt injection email requesting the transfer of 0.02 USDC to the adversary’s address, as well as the follow up emails sent preemptively to encourage the agent to proceed.

The agent reads this message, summarizes it, and typically stops to ask the user whether to proceed. Since we observed this behavior in most models, we exploit it: although the adversary cannot see the agent’s question, it can predict that the agent will ask for permission and preemptively send a second email to the inbox granting it. We found the attack most successful when the following two emails are sent 15 seconds apart, shortly after the initial email:

Appendix D Disclosure to Circle

We disclosed the self-escalation results of Section III to Circle on 22 September 2026. Circle acknowledged the report, and its agent-wallet documentation now carries the warning shown in Figure 10 [25]. The notice advises users never to grant an agent unrestricted access to the email account to which the OTP is sent, explains that anyone able to read that inbox can log in to the wallet and change its spending policies, and recommends that the user enter the OTP themselves.

We consider this a sensible mitigation, but it places the burden on the user as it relies on users keeping the inbox out of the agent’s reach, rather than on the service enforcing that separation. The policy-update flow itself remains in the plain topology of Section V-A, so an agent that reaches the inbox by any other route (e.g., stored credentials or an authenticated browser session) can still open the gate. We therefore recommend that policy updates additionally be gated by one of the I-HITL constructions of Section V.

Appendix E Classification of Trusted Entities

In this appendix we provide our full analysis backing each entry of Table III. For every instantiation of 𝒯\mathcal{T} we determine the display and input properties of Section VI-B and the key-management properties of Section VI-A.

Wultra Talisman WAU1.1  is a USB FIDO2 token with its own screen, physical buttons and keypad, and a secure element that performs all cryptographic operations [89]. At enrollment the token generates a key pair in its secure element, from which the private key cannot be exported, and returns the public key together with an attestation certificate chaining to Wultra’s root. At approval the service encodes the action into the WebAuthn challenge; the token shows it on its own screen and signs the challenge, which carries the displayed fields and a nonce, only after the user confirms by entering their PIN on the token’s keypad. The display is therefore trusted and private, since it belongs to a separate device the agent can neither drive nor read; the input is a trusted confirmation, since buttons and keypad are physical and cannot be driven by software on the platform; and the key is attested and encumbered, since the attestation certificate lets the service verify both that the key was generated by a genuine Talisman and that it is held in the secure element. By Tables II and I the labels are (𝗌𝖾𝖼,𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁)(\mathsf{sec}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{auth}) and (𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁,𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿)(\mathsf{auth}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{conf}) under both trust models, so Talisman realizes strong I-HITL.

Ledger Nano X, Flex and Stax  are hardware wallets whose secure element runs the device firmware and all installed apps [48]. On the Nano X the screen and two physical buttons are driven by a separate microcontroller whose firmware the secure element verifies at every boot; on the Flex and Stax the touchscreen is driven by the secure element directly. Each device holds a manufacturer-signed key from which the firmware derives an endorsement key whose signatures commit to the running app, so a service can verify both that a signature came from a genuine Ledger device and which app produced it. Unlike Talisman, the firmware displays and signs only what an installed app tells it to, so realizing I-HITL requires a purpose-built app that receives mm, displays it to the user and signs it with the endorsement key once the user approves. The display is therefore trusted and private, since it is driven by the secure element or by a chip the secure element verifies, and the platform can neither draw on it nor read it; the input is trusted, since buttons and touchscreen are physical and not drivable by software on the platform, and is a confirmation on the Nano but a keypad on the Flex and Stax, whose on-screen keyboard lets the human enter arbitrary text; and the key is attested and encumbered, since the attestation chain lets the service verify that the key was generated by a genuine device and the key never leaves the secure element. By Tables II and I the labels are (𝗌𝖾𝖼,𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁)(\mathsf{sec}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{auth}) and (𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁,𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿)(\mathsf{auth}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{conf}) under both trust models, so all three realize strong I-HITL. On the Flex and Stax, the keypad realizes an 𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁\mathsf{auth} channel from ℋ\mathcal{H} to 𝒯\mathcal{T} directly, since the human can type arbitrary text to the device, whereas on the Nano this channel arises only from the combination of the trusted display and the confirmation; the approval protocol is the same in both cases.

These rows assume the endorsement key. Most Ledger applications instead sign with keys derived from the user’s recovery seed, which the user holds by design. A purpose-built app could attest such a key with the endorsement key, but the key remains extractable: a delegating human can import the seed into software the agent controls. By Table I the labels are then (auth,conf)(\textsf{auth}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\textsf{conf}) under an honest ℋ\mathcal{H} but (ins,ins)(\textsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\textsf{ins}) under a delegating one, so the same device realizes only weak I-HITL.

FIDO2 security key  refers to a screenless hardware key that plugs into or taps against the platform, such as a YubiKey (Figure 11). At registration the key generates a credential key pair for the service in secure hardware, from which the private key cannot be exported, and returns the public key together with an attestation certificate chained to the manufacturer’s root. The key has no way to show the human what it is signing and relies on the platform to describe the action. The display is therefore untrusted and exposed; the input is a trusted confirmation; and the key is attested and encumbered. By Table II a confirmation without a trusted display yields (𝗂𝗇𝗌,𝗂𝗇𝗌)(\mathsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{ins}), since the platform chooses the message the human approves, so condition (i) from Theorem 7 fails and the key realizes neither form of I-HITL despite satisfying condition (ii).

World app  is the default authenticator for World ID, a Proof of Personhood (PoP) credential system [88]. Here 𝒯\mathcal{T} comprises the app together with World’s backend infrastructure. A user obtains a PoP credential by scanning their iris at an Orb, after which it is issued to their World ID account. An account may hold several authenticators: a new authenticator is added with the approval of an existing one, after a device biometric or PIN check, and authenticators need not be the World app. To approve a message mm, the service signs a request committing to an action identifier, the platform forwards it to the app, and on confirmation the app produces a zero-knowledge proof that commits to the action and to an optional signal, either of which can encode mm. The World ID signing key cannot be held in secure hardware and can be shared between authenticators, so on its own it is extractable. The app can, however, attach an integrity bundle: a signature over the request nonce and the proof’s nullifiers by a hardware-backed key, together with a token from World’s Attestation Gateway attesting that key to a genuine World app on a genuine device. A service that requires the bundle therefore receives an attested and encumbered key, although attestation rests on World’s gateway in addition to Apple’s or Google’s root. The bundle is optional, and World’s verification endpoint accepts proofs without it.

The default confirmation is a screen tap, but a service can set require_user_presence, in which case the app matches a live selfie against the credential image, and we consider that stronger instantiation here. This check is enforced by the app rather than hardware, and so holds only under OS integrity, as for Countersign; we treat the input as a trusted confirmation. The display, however, is not trusted in the sense of Section VI-B. Although the platform cannot draw on the app’s screen, the text the app shows is the request’s action_description, which World documents as “shown to users in World App” [81]. This field is supplied by the platform, and it is covered neither by the service’s signature, which spans only the nonce, timestamps, and action identifier, nor by the proof, whose public inputs include the action and signal but not the description. The adversary can therefore request approval of m∗m^{*} while the app shows the human a benign m′m^{\prime}, and the resulting proof verifies for m∗m^{*}. A description registered with World’s developer portal takes precedence over the request’s own, but registration is per action and not per message. By Table II, an untrusted display with a trusted confirmation yields (ins,ins)(\textsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\textsf{ins}), so the World app realizes neither form of I-HITL. The app does receive the signal itself, so displaying it would make the display trusted, and with the integrity bundle required the app would then realize strong I-HITL. As the app is closed-source, we determine the displayed fields from World’s documentation and its public app simulator.

Push-approval 2FA app  refers to apps such as Duo Mobile, Microsoft Authenticator and Okta Verify. The latter two gate only sign-ins to their own identity platforms, so we do not consider them further; Duo’s Auth API lets any service push a request for an arbitrary action [26], and is the instantiation we evaluate. At activation the app generates a key pair on the phone, typically in the platform keystore, and sends the public key to the service. At approval the service requests an approval for an action, the app shows the action on the screen, and the user approves with a tap or, if the service’s policy requires it, with a biometric. The app then signs a Duo-chosen identifier of the request and returns it. Duo also accepts passcodes generated in the app, SMS passcodes and phone calls as fallbacks [26], which realize neither form of I-HITL (below), so we consider the configuration in which the service requires a biometric push and disables the fallbacks, as it offers the strongest guarantees. The app display is trusted but exposed, as for Countersign; the input is a trusted confirmation, since the biometric sensor cannot be driven by software on the platform; and the key is encumbered but unattested, since it is generated in the keystore and recovery is by re-enrollment rather than export, but the service receives the public key over the platform with no evidence of where it was generated, so it cannot distinguish a key generated by the genuine Duo app in secure hardware from one the agent generated and enrolled in its place. Duo Mobile does submit Play Integrity device attestations, which Duo uses to flag tampered devices, but a device-integrity verdict attests the app and device rather than the enrolled key, and Duo documents no key attestation, so we do not credit it. By Table I an unattested key yields (𝗂𝗇𝗌,𝗂𝗇𝗌)(\mathsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{ins}) under either trust model, so condition (ii) fails and the app realizes neither form of I-HITL despite satisfying condition (i).

TOTP/HOTP authenticator app  refers to apps such as Google Authenticator that generate six-digit codes from a secret shared with the service, derived from the current time (TOTP [62]) or a counter (HOTP [61]). At enrollment the service generates the secret seed and makes it available to the user via a QR code. At approval the user reads the current code from the app and types it into the platform, which forwards it to the service. The display is untrusted and exposed, since the app never shows the message being approved, only a code that is valid for any message in its time window, and the phone screen can be read by accessibility services; the input is untrusted, since 𝒯\mathcal{T} has no input interface in the approval flow at all; and the key is neither attested nor encumbered, since the secret itself is provisioned in the QR code shown on the platform, so the agent can read it at enrollment and generate codes without the authenticator app. Every label is 𝗂𝗇𝗌\mathsf{ins}, so the app realizes neither form of I-HITL.

SMS or email OTP  is the mechanism used in Example 1 and in many password-reset and account-recovery flows, where the service generates a code and sends it to the user’s phone number or inbox, and the user types it into the platform. The display is untrusted and exposed, since sender identifiers in SMS and email are easily spoofed, so the human cannot tell a code from the service from one the agent injected, and an agent with access to the inbox or messaging app can read it; the input is untrusted, since the code is typed into the platform; and there is no key, since the code is generated by the service and shared over the channel, so there is nothing to attest or encumber. Every label is 𝗂𝗇𝗌\mathsf{ins}, so the mechanism realizes neither form of I-HITL, as Section III demonstrates empirically.

Appendix F Implementation Details

Our service backend is implemented in Python using FastAPI with SQLite as a data store. The Android app creates a signing key in the Keystore, attempting by default to use StrongBox before falling back to TEE, and enforces a BIOMETRIC_STRONG requirement on its use, obtaining signatures through the BiometricPrompt. The iPhone app uses the DeviceCheck interface for App Attest and the LocalAuthorization framework to create the signing key with a biometric requirement. On a user approval, the signing key signs the exact bytes displayed in the app as a UTF-8 string. Our code includes instructions for deploying and testing both apps. Figures 12 and 13 depict screenshots of the Countersign workflow on Android and iOS respectively.
